title: Taste Buds of the Righteous Mind
coreMove: Name the moral receptor that fired before arguing about whether the reaction is reasonable.
sourcePressure: The chapter makes moral plurality concrete through the taste-buds metaphor and several kinds of moral trigger.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer lists foundations like vocabulary words instead of making moral receptors feel active in scenes.

sourceAnchors.name: moral taste buds
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says the chapter makes moral plurality concrete through the taste receptor comparison.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The taste-buds image lets a reader hear a rival's concern as another receptor firing, not as a defect in the tongue.

sourceAnchors.name: moral triggers
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says people respond to several kinds of moral trigger rather than only harm and fairness.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A trigger does not have to convince the whole mind first; it only has to touch the receptor built to notice it.

hook: Do not open ch06 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: airport security training after inconsistent passenger judgments
exampleSpecs.audience: trainers teaching staff to name moral triggers
exampleSpecs.stakes: Rachel labels authority, harm, and fairness triggers before correcting officers.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Rachel replays three lane incidents and has officers tag the receptor before debating the call.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The training room screen freezes on a suitcase halfway through the scanner.

exampleSpecs.domain: sports league discipline panel reviewing taunting, cheating, and injury
exampleSpecs.audience: volunteer panel members with mixed reactions
exampleSpecs.stakes: Nicolas sorts the cases by receptor rather than penalty size.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Nicolas asks whether each outrage comes from harm, fairness, loyalty, or authority before setting sanctions.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Why does the cheap shot feel different from the fake roster?" Nicolas asks.

exampleSpecs.domain: nursing home staff deciding whether a family ritual can stay
exampleSpecs.audience: care staff balancing safety and dignity
exampleSpecs.stakes: Giulia names sanctity and care triggers in the same room.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Giulia moves the incense discussion from rule violation to competing moral receptors.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A thin line of incense smoke curls above the plastic medication cart.

exampleSpecs.domain: online game moderation team judging betrayal inside player guilds
exampleSpecs.audience: moderators who see only rule violations
exampleSpecs.stakes: Kiran distinguishes fairness cheating from loyalty betrayal in player complaints.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Kiran tags the complaints and changes which cases get mediation instead of bans.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Kiran twenty player tickets to see that betrayal had its own taste.

exampleSpecs.domain: food co-op board debating supplier standards
exampleSpecs.audience: board members whose moral concerns talk past each other
exampleSpecs.stakes: Lars maps purity, harm, and fairness before choosing criteria.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Which receptor is firing when Lars refuses a supplier that meets every safety rule?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Which concern remains after the lab results come back clean?

exampleSpecs.domain: architecture firm reviewing a courthouse redesign
exampleSpecs.audience: designers navigating authority, access, and dignity
exampleSpecs.stakes: Paula treats the building complaints as different moral receptors, not aesthetic preferences.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Paula mark which comments seek openness, which seek dignity, and which seek authority.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You stand over a model courthouse with removable stone steps.

skillTargets: identify which moral receptor a scene activates
distinguish a trigger from a reasoned conclusion
use the taste-buds metaphor without treating it as literal biology

tryThisNowSpec: When a reaction feels disproportionate, label the receptor it touched before deciding whether the reaction was justified.
